item.title: IPMAN: Importance-based Pruning of Multiverse Analysis visualizatioN
item.description: arXiv:2611.31563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiverse analysis has been proposed as a means to transparently communicate the influence of methodological decisions and their combinations on empirical outcomes. However, scholars warn that the method can be misleading when the methodological decisions are de-emphasized and the wide distribution of estimates from various decisions is interpreted out of context as ammunition to attack social science research for being non-robust. The potential for the misuse of multiverse analysis is exacerbated by the weaknesses of the current reporting methods of multiverse analysis, mostly via the two mainstream ways of data visualization: density plot and specification curve. The former completely neglects methodological choices, while the latter becomes messy even with only a few methodological decisions, as the number of elements to be plotted at least doubles when one decision is added. In this article, we propose a visualization method that is based on pruning a full decision tree, such that the most important decisions remain. The visualization can communicate what methodological decision combinations lead to systematic changes in estimates inside a multiverse. Our visualization scales well even when many methodological decisions are considered and avoids common misinterpretations of existing reporting standards. We argue that multiverse analysis and its visualizations should be considered as an opportunity to obtain a deeper understanding of how an empirical outcome is generated out of many methodological decisions. Our proposed visualization method fulfills this purpose and communicate robustness of empirical findings in an equitable manner.
item.dc:creator: Maximilian Linde, Jun Sun, Chung-hong Chan

item.title: Dynamic Emulation for Bayesian Inverse Problems in Spatiotemporal Mechanistic Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.31695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Calibrating a spatiotemporal mechanistic model to field data is a Bayesian inverse problem in which every likelihood evaluation needs a simulator run. The R package *spDBL* replaces the simulator with a dynamic emulator, a matrix-variate dynamic linear model with a closed-form posterior that evolves the field in discrete time and processes large grids in spatial blocks. It then calibrates the parameters without further simulator runs, using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (implemented in the Stan programming environment) conditionally on emulator draws. In benchmarks on epidemic fields, with every method tuned alike, *spDBL*'s predictions at untried inputs were the only ones with near-nominal interval coverage, though a tuned *RobustGaSP* was more accurate, and *spDBL*'s calibrations matched the accuracy of *RobustCalibration* with higher, though below nominal, interval coverage (80% against 67-76%) and over 50 times more effective samples per CPU second.
item.dc:creator: Xiang Chen, Sudipto Banerjee

item.title: recurcast: Coherent Forecasts for History-Dependent Recurrent and Terminal Events in R
item.description: arXiv:2611.32075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers studying recurrent events and terminal outcomes need software that connects incomplete event histories to interpretable forecasts and uncertainty estimates. We present recurcast, an R package for fitting history-dependent recurrent and terminal event models, predicting future event burden and terminal-event risk, and assessing sensitivity to incomplete observation. Users supply event histories, covariates and observation information; the package returns fitted models, dynamic forecasts, uncertainty summaries and diagnostic measures under explicitly stated assumptions. The package integrates over event histories compatible with tied dates or observation windows and supports several frailty distributions for between-subject heterogeneity. A shared probability model generates recurrent-event counts, terminal-event probabilities and restricted mean time alive. Cross-fitted targeting provides influence-function diagnostics and asymptotic inference in supported missing-at-random and right-censoring settings. Separate sensitivity analyses provide bounds under specified recording restrictions. A baseline binary-treatment interface estimates standardized treatment contrasts under consistency, conditional exchangeability, positivity and independent censoring. A C++17 computational core supports the R interface. Independent numerical checks, computational benchmarks, simulation experiments and reproducible examples document accuracy, performance and inferential limitations. Outputs retain observation assumptions, convergence information and numerical diagnostics. The package, tutorials and replication materials are publicly available, supporting transparent analysis across clinical and other event-history applications.
item.dc:creator: Sunday A. Adetunji, Oluwatimileyin A. Adetunji

item.title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.32430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many real-world interactions involve groups of nodes rather than pairs. A non-uniform hypergraph records such interactions as hyperedges of different orders, where the order counts the nodes in a hyperedge. Full estimation evaluates every candidate hyperedge, whose number grows exponentially with the order, and classical remedies sacrifice higher-order information or aggravate computation. The orders are not isolated: the lower orders, cheap to compute and rich in information, reveal where higher-order hyperedges are likely to occur. We propose CINE (Cross-order Information-guided Negative-sampling Estimation) under a latent space model in which all orders share latent positions. Starting from order two, CINE climbs one order at a time. At each higher order, CINE keeps all present hyperedges, samples a small subset of negative examples guided by lower-order scores, and corrects for the known inclusion probabilities to preserve the target of full estimation. CINE thereby lets users choose the trade-off between computation time and estimation accuracy: the retained orders and the sampling budget set the time, and the retained information provably approaches full-data information as the sampling budget grows. In simulations, CINE approaches the accuracy of full estimation at a small fraction of its computation time, and larger teams in MADStat reveal research associations.
item.dc:creator: Rongzhuo Nie, Menghao Wang, Sanguo Zhang, Mingyang Ren, Guojun Zhu

item.title: Exact local queries for pseudo-marginal Markov chains
item.description: arXiv:2611.32955v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local queries of a Markov chain can depend on past updates outside the queried components. For pseudo-marginal chains with Gaussian graph priors, we construct decision certificates from finite historical parameter ranges to settle updates before all neighbouring records are resolved. Under shared random inputs and exact arithmetic, the executor recovers the reference parameters, auxiliary variables and likelihood estimates for any prespecified finite query sequence. We bound conditional expected work, including likelihood evaluation, historical range construction and execution management. On specified path and grid families, we fix per-node history lengths and all other parameters in the work bounds. As graph size grows, expected incremental work stays bounded for certificate execution and grows linearly for the specified cached pointwise evaluator answering the same query. In controlled experiments, certificate execution is faster than pointwise and parallel Picard execution for sparse queries, whereas Picard is faster than certificate execution for full queries. We apply the method to positron emission tomography and Gaussian process classification of Landmine data. For a fixed numerical tomography posterior, certificate execution completes all queries of regional mean distribution volume within budget, while full execution completes none from the same initial cache. In Landmine, posterior summaries of the difference in log length scales between two sites agree across pseudo-marginal and ancillary augmentation samplers within estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty. Certificate execution resolves almost every scheduled update over the full query sequence.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Xu

item.title: Local subspace encoding for spectral prediction: from TabPFN to operator-adaptive calibration
item.description: arXiv:2611.31245v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: TabPFN has already shown useful predictive performance on near-infrared spectra. RamanPFN subsequently proposed two spectral representations for tabular inference: Global Compositional Unmixing (GCU) and Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding (LVSE). We assess whether these representations also help on datasets assembled through the nirs4all ecosystem, and whether their value extends to classical calibration. We reanalyse completed experiments from a public spectral dataset catalogue. On a post-hoc subset of 61 matched numerical prediction tasks, after excluding ten class-code, metadata or semantically ambiguous targets, LVSE reduces RMSE relative to raw-spectrum TabPFN by 10.22%, 12.80% and 14.52% on average for checkpoints 2.5, 3 and 3.5, respectively, with median reductions of 4.99%, 4.74% and 7.82%. Across 76 classification datasets, weighted F1 increases by 2.22, 2.56 and 3.81 percentage points. The 2.5 classification procedure uses output coding on 15 datasets exceeding the checkpoint's native class limit. GCU alone is less reliable in this implementation. LVSE also improves PLS and Ridge in many cases, with median RMSE reductions of 4.75% and 1.89%. Adding LVSE candidates to an operator-adaptive model is feasible, but a separate 35-task panel derived from the public AOM benchmark shows only small median gains. These results motivate evaluating LVSE alongside existing representation choices. They do not establish that a selector choosing between raw and LVSE inputs will improve every task.
item.dc:creator: Gregory Beurier, Robin Reiter, Denis Cornet, Lauriane Rouan

item.title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.31687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent advances in stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) have enabled efficient online optimization, existing methods either rely on gradient information or suffer from high computational costs. To address these limitations, we develop a sketched derivative-free SSQP (SDF-SSQP) method that simultaneously achieves computational efficiency and valid statistical inference. By leveraging randomized sketching, the proposed method reduces the per-iteration computational cost to $O((d+m)^2)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision variable and $m$ is the number of constraints, making it well suited for large-scale problems. To overcome the challenges that both sketching and zeroth-order approximations introduce for statistical inference, we adopt a random-scaling approach that eliminates the need for explicit estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix. We establish the asymptotic normality of the averaged primal--dual iterates and construct a self-normalized statistic that is asymptotically pivotal. The resulting inference procedure is fully online, requires neither covariance estimation nor matrix inversion, and incurs an additional per-iteration cost of the same order as that of the optimization update. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both optimization performance and statistical inference accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Jianliang Ye, Sen Na

item.title: Beyond Classical Minimax Rates: Quantum Sampling in Gradient-Based Simulation Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.32004v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study gradient-based search for a class of convex simulation optimization problems with gradients estimated from noisy outputs. With independent outputs, the optimal classical convergence rate for the expected objective gap is of order $O(N^{-2/3})$, where $N$ is the query budget. We apply quantum mean estimation to paired finite differences and progressively increase their estimation accuracy as the perturbations shrink, improving the convergence rate to $O(N^{-4/3})$. Furthermore, we show that coupling nearby evaluations improves the classical and quantum convergence rates to $O(N^{-2/(3-\kappa)})$ and $O(N^{-4/(3-\kappa)})$, respectively, where $\kappa\in[0,1]$ describes the variance reduction in paired outputs. Thus, quantum estimation halves the accuracy exponent in query complexity across coupling orders. Moreover, we establish matching lower bounds and show that these accuracy exponents are minimax optimal for fixed decision dimension, even when query locations and batch sizes are adaptive. Reconstruction from feasible differences retains the exponents when every simulation query must be feasible and accommodates boundary optima.
item.dc:creator: Hao Cao, Jian-Qiang Hu, Mingjie Hu, Qixin Wang

item.title: Breaking Resonance: Square-root acceleration for Metropolis-adjusted randomized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
item.description: arXiv:2611.32322v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with a fixed integration time can fail to mix because of resonances, and randomizing the integration time removes them. We prove that Metropolis-adjusted HMC with velocity Verlet and random integration times mixes from a warm start in a number of transitions that does not depend on the condition number, for every integration-time law satisfying a Fourier condition that we call non-resonant; uniform, exponential and triangular laws are examples. For a target density proportional to $e^{-U}$ on $\mathbb R^d$, where $U$ is $m$-strongly convex with $L$-Lipschitz gradient and $L_H$-Lipschitz Hessian and $\kappa=L/m$, the number of gradient evaluations needed to reach a fixed total variation accuracy is, up to constants and logarithmic factors, $\sqrt{\kappa d}+\sqrt{L_H}\,(d/m)^{3/4}$. This is the first square-root condition-number bound for this sampler beyond Gaussian targets. The proof converts relative-entropy contraction of the unadjusted proposal into a conductance bound for the adjusted chain, and shows that the integration-time law enters only through its characteristic function. Hessian regularity cannot be dropped for a fixed step size: without it there are targets in the class for which the cost is at least of order $\kappa^{2/3}$, up to logarithmic factors, even from a warm start.
item.dc:creator: Nawaf Bou-Rabee

item.title: Model-Based Clustering of Longitudinal Functional Data with Hidden Semi-Markov Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.32693v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Model-based clustering of longitudinal functional data must account both for heterogeneity among curves and for temporal dependence in their latent group memberships. Functional mixture models typically treat curves as exchangeable, while temporal approaches may restrict regime persistence or ignore state-specific functional variation. We propose hidden semi-Markov models for ordered sequences of multivariate functional observations in which each latent regime has a parsimonious, state-specific functional principal subspace, extending functional high-dimensional data clustering (funHDDC) to longitudinal settings. Gaussian, contaminated-Gaussian and multivariate-$t$ emissions accommodate atypical observations, and explicit state-specific sojourn distributions govern regime persistence, with hidden Markov models as the geometric special case. Estimation uses expectation-maximization (EM) and expectation/conditional-maximization (ECM) algorithms with segmental forward-backward recursions, and identifiability is established up to label permutations and spectral indeterminacies. In simulations, temporal dependence yields the largest gains when single curves are weakly informative; with robust emissions, state-specific subspaces outperform a global functional principal component representation; and explicit durations add smaller gains when regimes overlap and sojourns are non-geometric. Applications to air-quality profiles and smartphone activity recordings, evaluated on held-out years and subjects, show improved predictive fit and illustrate how apparent duration effects can reflect time-varying transitions.
item.dc:creator: Bagas Caesar Suherlan, Emilio Porcu, Antonello Maruotti

item.title: Visualizing the geometry of labeled high-dimensional data with spheres
item.description: arXiv:2107.00731v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data visualizations can summarize high-dimensional distributions in two or three dimensions. Dimensionality reduction entails a loss of information, and what is preserved differs between methods. Existing methods preserve the local or the global geometry of the points, and most techniques do not consider labels. Here we introduce "hypersphere2sphere" (H2S), a new method that aims to visualize not the points, but the relationships between the labeled distributions. H2S fits a hypersphere to each labeled set of points in the high-dimensional space of the original data and visualizes each hypersphere as a sphere in 3D (or a circle in 2D). H2S perfectly captures the geometry of up to 4 high-dimensional hyperspheres using spheres in 3D (or 3 using circles in 2D), and approximates the geometry for larger numbers of distributions, matching the sizes (radii), and the pairwise separations (between-center distances) and the overlaps (along the center-connection line). The resulting visualizations are robust to sampling imbalances. Leveraging labels and the sphere as the simplest geometrical primitive, H2S provides an important addition to the toolbox of visualization techniques.
item.dc:creator: Andrew D Zaharia, Anish S Potnis, Alexander Walther, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte

item.title: confoundvis: an R package for sensitivity analysis of risk differences and established robustness measures for unmeasured confounding
item.description: arXiv:2610.13731v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Observational studies of binary outcomes often lead to practical decisions. For example, does a treatment add a meaningful number of deaths per 100 patients? Sensitivity analysis asks how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be to change such a conclusion. Bringing an estimate down to a practically important size and bringing it to zero are different questions, and they can need very different confounders. We present the R package confoundvis, which stores any one-dimensional sensitivity analysis in a common object and applies the same plotting, reporting, and tabulation functions to it. Version 0.4.1 adds sens_risk_difference(), which applies the binary-confounder model of Lin, Psaty, and Kronmal to a fitted model. This function standardizes the risks to the study population and reports where the risk difference reaches a user-chosen threshold and where it reaches zero. The package also computes the omitted-variable-bias bounds of the Python package doubleml for fits from the R package DoubleML, imports instrumental-variable sensitivity analyses from iv.sensemakr, and runs partial R2, impact-threshold, replacement, E-value, and Rosenbaum analyses through one call. In the right heart catheterization data (5,735 patients), catheterization was associated with 6.3 more deaths within 30 days per 100 patients (95% CI 3.7 to 8.9). For a confounder present in 40% of catheterized and 20% of other patients, an odds ratio of 3.39 with death brought the difference down to an illustrative threshold of 2 deaths per 100. On the other hand, an odds ratio of 6.37 was needed to bring it to zero. All results agreed with the established implementations.
item.dc:creator: Subir Hait

item.title: Sequential Monte Carlo approximations of Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao gradient flows
item.description: arXiv:2506.05905v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider the problem of sampling from a probability distribution $\pi$. It is well known that this can be written as an optimisation problem over the space of probability distribution in which we aim to minimise the Kullback--Leibler divergence from $\pi$. We consider several partial differential equations (PDEs) whose solution is a minimiser of the Kullback--Leibler divergence from $\pi$ and connect them to well-known Monte Carlo algorithms. We focus in particular on PDEs obtained by considering the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry over the space of probabilities and show that these lead to a natural implementation using importance sampling and sequential Monte Carlo. We propose a novel algorithm to approximate the Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao flow of the Kullback--Leibler divergence and conduct an extensive empirical study to identify when this algorithm outperforms other popular Monte Carlo algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Francesca R. Crucinio, Sahani Pathiraja

item.title: Generalized Guarantees for Variational Inference in the Presence of Even and Elliptical Symmetry
item.description: arXiv:2511.01064v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Variational inference (VI) approximates a target density $p$ by the best match $q$ in a family $\mathcal Q$ of tractable distributions. The variational approximation is found by minimizing a divergence, most commonly the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence $\text{KL}(q||p)$, although other divergences can be considered. In practice, $p \notin \mathcal Q$ and so the optimal variational approximation is misspecified. Despite this misspecification, it was recently shown that the minimizer of $\text{KL}(q||p)$ is guaranteed to recover the mean in the presence of even symmetry and likewise the correlation matrix in the presence of elliptical symmetry for a log-concave target $p$. We extend this result in several directions. First, we relax the assumption of log-concavity and instead merely require $p$ to be unimodal, allowing for heavy-tailed targets. Second, we obtain guarantees for cases where $p$ exhibits symmetry along some but not all of its coordinates. These partial symmetries arise naturally in Bayesian hierarchical models, where the prior induces a challenging geometry but still possesses axes of symmetry. Third, we extend these guarantees to $f$-divergences, a broad class which includes the forward and reverse-KL divergences and the $\alpha$-divergences.
item.dc:creator: Charles C. Margossian, Isaac E. Rankin, Lawrence K. Saul

item.title: Exponential Smoothing for Time Series of Random Objects
item.description: arXiv:2609.20274v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Time series of random objects, such as covariance matrices, probability distributions, and functional data, call for forecasting methods that do not rely on arithmetic operations. We introduce geodesic exponential smoothing for time series in Hadamard spaces. The forecast level moves a fixed fraction of the way along the geodesic towards each new observation. The smoothing parameter is estimated by minimising the average squared distance between observations and forecasts. The method involves a single scalar parameter, assumes no stationarity, and updates online in constant time per observation. We further introduce an innovations mechanism under which each observation has conditional Fr\'echet mean equal to the current level, the metric-space analogue of the innovations state-space model. We show via the quasilinearisation of Hadamard spaces that the level is a martingale in a nonlinear sense, that the spread of the data from the initial state grows at least linearly in time, and that their quasi-autocorrelation at any fixed lag tends to one. We prove almost-sure consistency and asymptotic normality of the smoothing-parameter estimator. Three real-data applications, spanning covariance-matrix, distributional, and functional time series, assess the forecasting performance against structurally heavier alternatives.
item.dc:creator: Takuo Matsubara, Peiwen Jiang, Wilson Ye Chen, Minh-Ngoc Tran
